items.title: Fire Burns Without a Burner, and No Means of Knowledge Finds a Self Apart from Seeing

items.zh: 若言如火，則徒計於我，不應道理。何以故？如世間火，離能燒者亦自能燒故。若言離見者等相別有我者，則所計我相乖一切量，不應道理。
items.en: If you compare it to fire, then positing a self at all becomes pointless — this makes no sense. Why is this? Because worldly fire, even apart from any separate "burner" wielding it, burns entirely on its own. If, further, you posit a self entirely apart from the mark of "the seer" and the like, then the self you posit contradicts every means of valid knowledge — this makes no sense.

items.title: Defilement and Purity Need No Self Behind Them Either

items.zh: 又我今問汝，隨汝意答。汝所計我，為與染淨相應而有染淨？為不與染淨相應而有染淨耶？若與染淨相應而有染淨者，於諸行中，有疾疫災橫及彼止息順益可得，即彼諸行，雖無有我，而說有染淨相應。如於外物，內身亦爾。雖無有我，染淨義成。故汝計我，不應道理。
items.en: Further, I now ask you, answer as you see fit: does the self you posit have defilement and purity through association with defilement and purity, or without any such association at all? If through association, then note that among mere conditioned formations — with no self involved — one already finds sickness, calamity, and misfortune, as well as their cessation and benefit. Those very formations, though lacking any self, are already spoken of as associated with defilement and purity. As with external things, so too with this body: though there is no self, the meaning of defilement and purity is fully accounted for. Your positing a self for this purpose therefore makes no sense.

items.zh: 若不與染淨相應而有染淨者，離染淨相，我有染淨，不應道理。
items.en: If the self has defilement and purity without any association with defilement and purity at all, then a self having defilement and purity while entirely apart from the marks of defilement and purity makes no sense.

items.title: Cyclic Flow, Like a River or a Lamp's Flame, Needs No Self to Sustain It

items.zh: 又我今問汝，隨汝意答。汝所計我，為與流轉相相應而有流轉？為不與流轉相相應而有流轉及止息耶？若與流轉相相應而有流轉及止息者，於諸行中有五種流轉相可得。一、有因，二、可生，三、可滅，四、展轉相續生起，五、有變異。
items.en: Further, I now ask you, answer as you see fit: does the self you posit have cyclic flow through association with the mark of cyclic flow, or does it have flow and cessation without any such association? If through association, then among mere conditioned formations, five marks of cyclic flow are already found: first, having a cause; second, being capable of arising; third, being capable of ceasing; fourth, arising in continuous succession; fifth, undergoing change.

items.zh: 若諸行中，此流轉相可得，如於身、芽、河、燈、乘等流轉作用中，雖無有我，即彼諸行得有流轉及與止息，何須計我？若不與彼相相應而有流轉及止息者，則所計我無流轉相而有流轉止息，不應道理。
items.en: If these five marks of cyclic flow are already found among mere formations — as in the flowing activity of a body, a sprout, a river, a lamp's flame, or a moving vehicle — then, though no self is present, those very formations already have cyclic flow and cessation. What need, then, is there to posit a self at all? And if the self has flow and cessation without bearing the mark of flow at all, then a self with no mark of flow nonetheless having flow and cessation makes no sense.

items.title: Experiencer, Agent, and Liberated One — Does the Self Need to Change to Be Named These?

items.zh: 又我今問汝，隨汝意答。汝所計我，為由境界所生若苦若樂，及由思業，并由煩惱、隨煩惱等之所變異，說為受者、作者及解脫者？為不由彼變異，說為受者等耶？
items.en: Further, I now ask you, answer as you see fit: is your posited self called an experiencer, an agent, and one liberated because it undergoes change through pain or pleasure arising from its objects, through the karma of volition, and through root afflictions and secondary afflictions — or is it called these without undergoing any such change at all?

items.zh: 若由彼變異者，是即諸行是受者、作者及解脫者，何須計我？設是我者，我應無常，不應道理。若不由彼變異者，我無變異，而是受者、作者及解脫者，不應道理。
items.en: If through such change, then it is the formations themselves that are the experiencer, agent, and liberated one — what need is there to posit a self at all? And were this changing thing to be called a self, the self would have to be impermanent, which makes no sense given your own position. If without any such change at all, then something undergoing no change whatsoever nonetheless being called an experiencer, an agent, and one liberated makes no sense either.

items.title: If the Self Is the Universal "Agent," Why Does Anything Else Need to Act at All?

items.zh: 又汝今應說自所欲。為唯於我說為作者？為亦於餘法說為作者？
items.en: Further, you should now state what you actually intend: is only the self ever spoken of as the agent, or are other phenomena also spoken of as agents?

items.title: Universal Agency Collapses, and Even the Word "I" Never Actually Names a Self

items.zh: 若唯於我，世間不應說火為燒者，光為照者。若亦於餘法，即於見等諸根說為作者，徒分別我，不應道理。
items.en: If only the self is ever an agent, then the world should never speak of fire as "the burner" or light as "the illuminator" — yet it plainly does. If other phenomena are also agents, then one may as well simply call the sense-faculties themselves — seeing and the rest — the agents; positing a separate self for this purpose serves no purpose and makes no sense.

items.zh: 又汝應說自意所欲。為唯於我建立於我？為亦於餘法建立於我？若唯於我者，世間不應於彼假說士夫身呼為德友、佛授等。若亦於餘法者，是則唯於諸行假說名我，何須更執別有我耶？何以故？諸世間人唯於假設士夫之身起有情想，立有情名，及說自他有差別故。
items.en: Further, you should state what you actually intend: is the word "self" applied only to a genuine self, or is it also applied to other phenomena? If only to a genuine self, then the world should never apply it to a merely conventionally designated person, calling them "Guṇamitra" or "Buddhadatta" and the like — yet it plainly does. If it is also applied to other phenomena, then "self" is simply a conventional name provisionally given to the formations themselves — what need, then, is there to insist on some further, separate self? Why is this? Because everyone in the world, without exception, forms the notion of "a being," gives it the name "being," and speaks of self and other as different, entirely on the basis of a merely conventionally designated person.

items.title: The Decisive Question: Is Believing in a Self Wholesome, or Not?

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？計我之見為善？為不善耶？若是善者，何為極愚癡人深起我見？不由方便，率爾而起？能令眾生怖畏解脫，又能增長諸惡過失？不應道理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: is the view positing a self wholesome, or unwholesome? If wholesome, then why do even the most foolish beings hold this view most deeply, spontaneously and without any deliberate effort at all? Why does it make beings dread liberation itself, and cause every kind of unwholesome fault to grow? None of this makes sense for a genuinely wholesome view.

items.zh: 若不善者，不應說正及非顛倒。若是邪倒，所計之我體是實有，不應道理。
items.en: If unwholesome, then you should not go on calling it correct and undistorted. And if it is indeed a distorted, mistaken view, then insisting that the self it posits truly, substantially exists makes no sense at all.

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？無我之見為善？為不善耶？若言是善，於彼常住實有我上見無有我，而是善性。非顛倒計，不應道理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: is the view of no-self wholesome, or unwholesome? If you say it is wholesome, then seeing no self within what you call a permanent, truly existing self is itself wholesome and not a distorted view — which means your own belief in a self must be the distorted one; this contradicts your own position.

items.zh: 若言不善，而一切智者之所宣說，精勤方便之所生起，令諸眾生不怖解脫，能速證得白淨之果，諸惡過失如實對治，不應道理。
items.en: If you say it is unwholesome, then note: it is precisely what every possessor of complete wisdom teaches; it arises only through diligent effort and skilful means; it frees beings from dread of liberation; it swiftly brings about pure, wholesome results; and it genuinely counteracts every unwholesome fault. None of this fits an unwholesome view — so this makes no sense either.

items.title: The Final Dilemma, and Ten Angles Together Close the Case Against a Self

items.zh: 又汝意云何？為即我性自計有我？為由我見耶？若即我性自計有我者，應一切時無無我覺。若由我見者，雖無實我，由我見力故。於諸行中妄謂有我，是故汝計定實有我，不應道理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually think: does the self's own nature give rise to the notion of self, or does self-view give rise to it? If the self's own nature gives rise to it, then there should never be, at any time, a realisation of no-self — yet many do realise this. If self-view gives rise to it, then, though there is no real self, the mere force of self-view causes one to mistakenly suppose a self exists within the formations — and so your insistence that a self truly, definitely exists makes no sense.

items.zh: 如是不覺為先而起彼覺故，思覺為先見有所作故，於諸蘊中假施設故，由於彼相安立為有故，建立雜染及清淨故，建立流轉及止息故，假立受者、作者解脫者故，施設有作者故，施設言說故，施設見故，計有實我皆不應理。
items.en: Thus — whether by the spontaneous sense arising without prior deliberation; by deliberate intention preceding action; by mere provisional designation upon the aggregates; by positing existence through the mark of "the seer"; by positing defilement and purity; by positing cyclic flow and cessation; by positing an experiencer, agent, and liberated one; by positing an agent generally; by positing verbal convention; or by positing a view — through every one of these approaches, holding that a real self truly exists does not accord with reason.

blocks.text: Today completes the refutation of a self. After showing that a self is not found in perception, the treatise answers the deeper worry: without a self, who is defiled and purified, who wanders in saṃsāra, who experiences results and attains liberation? Each answer is the same: the formations, the impermanent processes of body and mind, are enough. The last argument asks a practical question: is believing in a self good for beings or not?

Perhaps the self is like fire, which burns things? But "worldly fire, even apart from any separate 'burner' wielding it, burns entirely on its own." Fire is a process; it needs fuel and conditions, not an owner. A self apart from seeing also "contradicts every means of valid knowledge". Master Cháng Bǎi: it is not perceived, it cannot be inferred, and scripture teaches non-self.

subs.head: Defilement and purity without a self

blocks.text: "Among mere conditioned formations, with no self involved, one already finds sickness, calamity, and misfortune, as well as their cessation and benefit." A plant can be blighted and recover; so can a body and mind. Defilement and purification are changes in the stream, not things that happen to someone behind it.

Saṃsāra itself needs no self. The formations already have five marks of flow: they have causes, they arise, they cease, they continue in succession, and they change. The treatise's examples: the body, a sprout, a river, a lamp's flame, a vehicle. A river is the same river from day to day though no water stays; a flame passes from wick to wick. Master Cháng Bǎi: the body's movements belong to one's own aggregates; the other examples are external, showing that the same pattern holds everywhere.

Isn't a self needed as the one who experiences, acts, and is freed? These names arise "through change": by pleasure and pain, by volitional karma, and by afflictions. Venerable Miào Jìng maps them onto the familiar triad of **affliction, karma, and suffering** (惑業苦). But "if through such change, then it is the formations themselves that are the experiencer, agent, and liberated one; what need is there to posit a self?" And a self that changed in these ways would be impermanent.

Is only the self called an agent? No: the world calls fire "the burner" and light "the illuminator". Venerable Miào Jìng: "The hand grasps, the foot walks, the mind thinks; these are all agents." When people say "I" or use a name, they refer to a person **conventionally designated** on the aggregates. Master Cháng Bǎi: "on the five aggregates a person is provisionally named, this one Zhang San, that one Li Si."

subs.head: Is believing in a self wholesome?

blocks.text: The decisive question. If self-view were wholesome, why do "even the most foolish beings hold this view most deeply, spontaneously"? Why does it make beings dread liberation and cause every fault to grow? No-self view, by contrast, is taught by all the omniscient, arises only through effort, frees beings from that dread, and counters every fault. Venerable Miào Jìng on how deep self-attachment runs: ants keep to their path even after you block it with water.

The refutation closes: from the two reasons and eight ways of positing a self, ten angles in all, "clinging to a real self makes no sense". Hán Qīngjìng's *Pīxún jì* uses these ten as the headings of the outline.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, why does likening the self to fire make positing a self pointless?
options: worldly fire burns by itself, apart from any "burner"
quiz.why: "Because worldly fire, even apart from any separate 'burner' wielding it, burns entirely on its own." Master Cháng Bǎi: "Fire in the world burns even without a person; fire burns by itself." Venerable Miào Jìng: using fire as the analogy "amounts to denying the self you cling to."

quiz.q: The text says a self apart from the seer "contradicts every means of valid knowledge." How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain?
options: it contradicts perception (unseen), inference (unprovable), and scripture (which teaches no-self)
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "It contradicts perception — it can't be seen; inference — reasoning can't establish it; scripture — the sages teach no-self." Venerable Miào Jìng: "The sages all rebuke 'self' and praise 'no-self.'" (The text's sickle analogy is untranslated in the Ru-Yi version, so no question is set on it.)

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what five marks of cyclic flow are found among the formations?
options: having a cause, able to arise, able to cease, arising in continuous succession, undergoing change
quiz.why: "First, having a cause; second, being capable of arising; third, being capable of ceasing; fourth, arising in continuous succession; fifth, undergoing change." Master Cháng Bǎi on the fourth: with countless conditions, the aggregates arise and cease each instant, the next following at once. With these five, formations flow by themselves — "what need for a self?"

quiz.q: The text says experiencer, agent, and liberated one are named through change by pain/pleasure, volitional karma, and afflictions. What does Venerable Miào Jìng map them to?
options: affliction, karma, suffering — afflictions are 惑, volitional karma 業, pain and pleasure 苦
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Afflictions and secondary afflictions are delusion, volitional karma is karma, experiencing pain and pleasure is suffering — delusion, karma, suffering." The text: if through such change, the formations themselves are experiencer, agent, and liberated — why posit a self? and a changing self would be impermanent. Master Cháng Bǎi: one calls the self experiencer as feelings change, liberated as afflictions end.

quiz.q: If only the self is an agent, what ordinary expressions does the text use to refute this?
options: the world calls fire "the burner" and light "the illuminator"
quiz.why: "If only the self is ever an agent, then the world should never speak of fire as 'the burner' or light as 'the illuminator.'" Venerable Miào Jìng: it is people who burn things with fire, yet they say fire is powerful and burns — so "agent" doesn't belong to a self alone.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what makes it absurd to call self-view wholesome?
options: the most foolish hold it deeply and spontaneously; it makes beings dread liberation; it grows every fault
quiz.why: "Why do even the most foolish beings hold this view most deeply, spontaneously and without any deliberate effort at all? Why does it make beings dread liberation itself, and cause every kind of unwholesome fault to grow?" Master Cháng Bǎi: liberation is no-self, so those attached "fear losing the self"; "Why do beings do all kinds of evil? For the sake of the self."

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what qualities of no-self view show it cannot be unwholesome?
options: taught by all the omniscient, arising through diligent effort, freeing beings from dread of liberation, swiftly bringing pure results, truly countering every fault
quiz.why: "It is precisely what every possessor of complete wisdom teaches; it arises only through diligent effort and skilful means; it frees beings from dread of liberation; it swiftly brings about pure, wholesome results; and it genuinely counteracts every unwholesome fault." Master Cháng Bǎi on "diligent effort": the right view of no-self arises only through calm and insight working together. Venerable Miào Jìng: no-self is not achieved just by saying it.
